# Soap (`soap`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by alkali_soda, lime_burning
- Core idea: Fat or oil boiled for hours with lye gives soap. Lye is made by letting water seep through hardwood ash; it becomes far stronger (caustic) if the ash is mixed with about a tenth of slaked lime. A floating egg was a rough density test; dissolved salts also float it, so it cannot establish how much caustic alkali is available to react. Potash lye gives soft soap; throwing salt into the hot mass, or using soda lye, gives hard bars. Many fats need roughly one part pure caustic soda to seven parts fat by mass; the actual amount depends on the fat and the strength of the lye.
- Pitfalls:
  - Too much lye: the soap burns the skin. Check free alkali by titration. Tasting can burn the mouth and curing cannot correct a substantial excess.
  - Lye splashes blind and burn; never boil it in aluminium, tin or lead vessels.
  - Thinking soap kills germs. It mainly lifts grease and dirt (and the germs in them) so that water carries them off.
  - Using softwood ash or rain-leached ash, which holds too little potash.
- History: mesopotamia: late 3rd millennium BC – Mesopotamian textile workers used oils and alkaline materials in cleaning wool; identifying a particular ancient mixture as finished soap is harder; egypt: c. 1550 BC – Ebers Papyrus mixes fats with alkaline salts for skin treatment; rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny describes sapo of tallow and ashes as a Gaulish hair pomade; soap for washing the body is attested from the 2nd c. AD (Galen); islamic: 7th–10th c. – hard olive-oil soap made with soda ash and lime in Aleppo and Nablus; al-Razi gives recipes; europe: 12th–15th c. – hard soap works in Castile, Marseille, Venice, Savona; 1791 Leblanc soda makes it cheap
- Read:
  - Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia XXVIII.191
  - F. W. Gibbs, The History of the Manufacture of Soap, Annals of Science 4 (1939)
  - Lewis Dartnell, The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Our World from Scratch (2014)
